and an isomorphism ZOut𝕀0⁡(P​Γˇ​(S))​(Inn⁡Γˇ​(S)/Inn⁡P​Γˇ​(S))≅Σ2×Σ2×GT^Z_{\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S))}(\operatorname{Inn}{\check{\Gamma}}(S)\left/\operatorname{Inn}{\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S)\right.)\cong\Sigma_{2}\times\Sigma_{2}\times\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}, so that, as above, we conclude that there is an isomorphism Out𝕀0⁡(Γˇ​(S))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}.

6.3. Lemma 6.3 implies (iii) and (iv) of Theorem 6.1

Let us first observe that [24, Theorem A] and its proof imply the following special case of items (iii) and (iv) of Theorem 6.1:

Lemma 6.4.

For S=S0,n1S=S^{1}_{0,n} and n≥4n\geq 4, there is a natural isomorphism:

Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))≅GT^,\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}},

such that GT^\widehat{\operatorname{GT}} acts on the center τδ1ℤ^\tau_{{\delta}_{1}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} of Γˇ​(S,∂S){\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}) through the character χλ:GT^→ℤ^∗\chi_{\lambda}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\to{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast}.

Proof.

Note that, in the notation of [24], we have Γˇ​(S,∂S)=B^n{\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})=\widehat{B}_{n} and Γˇ​(S)=ℬ^n{\check{\Gamma}}(S)=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{n}. Since τδ1ℤ^\tau_{{\delta}_{1}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} is a characteristic subgroup of Γˇ​(S,∂S){\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}), the natural epimorphism Γˇ​(S,∂S)→Γˇ​(S){\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})\to{\check{\Gamma}}(S) induces a homomorphism Aut⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Aut⁡(Γˇ​(S))\operatorname{Aut}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Aut}({\check{\Gamma}}(S)) which, by [24, Theorem 4.6], is surjective and whose kernel, as described in [24, Lemma 4.5], has trivial intersection with Aut𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})). Therefore, there is a natural isomorphism Aut𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))≅Aut𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\cong\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S)).

Since, by [24, Proposition 2.2 and Proposition 3.1], P​Γˇ​(S){\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S) is a characteristic subgroup of Γˇ​(S){\check{\Gamma}}(S), there is also a natural homomorphism Aut⁡(Γˇ​(S))→Aut⁡(P​Γˇ​(S))\operatorname{Aut}({\check{\Gamma}}(S))\to\operatorname{Aut}({\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S)) which, since the centralizer of Γˇ​(S){\check{\Gamma}}(S) in P​Γˇ​(S){\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S) is trivial (cf. for instance, [7, Theorem 4.14]), is injective.

By Lemma 3.13, we have that Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γˇ​(S))=Aut⁡(P​Γˇ​(S))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S))=\operatorname{Aut}({\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S)), which then implies that we have Aut𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))=Aut⁡(Γˇ​(S))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S))=\operatorname{Aut}({\check{\Gamma}}(S)) as well. By [24, Theorem 4.3, (i)], there is a natural isomorphism Out⁡(Γˇ​(S))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}({\check{\Gamma}}(S))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}. Combined with the previous isomorphisms, this yields the isomorphism, claimed in the lemma: Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}.

The last claim of the lemma then follows from the explicit description of this action given, for instance, in the appendix of [13]. ∎

Let us now observe that, given a nonseparating simple closed curve γ{\gamma} on SS, by the same construction of the homomorphism (7), where we use Theorem 2.7 and Theorem 2.8, instead of Theorem 2.3 and [3, Corollary 6.2], and Theorem 4.13 instead of Theorem 4.1, we get a natural homomorphism:

Rγ:Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S∖γ,∂S)).R_{\gamma}\colon\thinspace\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\partial S})).

For S=Sg,nkS=S_{g,n}^{k}, by composing gg of such homomorphisms, we get a natural homomorphism:

(16) R0:Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S0,n+2​gk,∂S)).R_{0}\colon\thinspace\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S_{0,n+2g}^{k},{\partial S})).
Lemma 6.5.

For d⁡(S)>1d(S)>1, the homomorphism R0R_{0} (16) is injective.

Proof.

There is a natural commutative diagram:

Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))×Aut⁡(A)↓R0↓Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S0,n+2​gk,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S0,n+2​gk))×Aut⁡(A),\begin{array}[]{ccc}\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))&\to&\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S))\times\operatorname{Aut}(A)\\ \;\downarrow\!\!{\scriptscriptstyle R_{0}}&&\downarrow\\ \operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S_{0,n+2g}^{k},{\partial S}))&\to&\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S_{0,n+2g}^{k}))\times\operatorname{Aut}(A),\end{array}

where A:=∏i=1kτδiℤ^A:=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\tau_{\delta_{i}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} identifies with the normal inertia subgroups of both groups Γˇ​(S,∂S){\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}) and Γˇ​(S0,n+2​gk,∂S){\check{\Gamma}}(S_{0,n+2g}^{k},{\partial S}). By (i) of Lemma 4.8, we have that both horizontal homomorphisms are injective. From the isomorphisms Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}} and Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S0,n+2​gk))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S_{0,n+2g}^{k}))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}} (cf. Section 6.2), it then follows that also the righthand vertical homomorphism is injective and so the lefthand vertical homomorphism R0R_{0} is injective too. ∎

Let R∅:Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))R_{\emptyset}\colon\thinspace\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S)) be the natural homomorphism defined in Section 4.4. We have:

Lemma 6.6.

For S=S0,nkS=S_{0,n}^{k} with n+k≥5n+k\geq 5 and k≥1k\geq 1, the natural homomorphism R∅:Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))R_{\emptyset}\colon\thinspace\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S)) is injective.

Proof.

By (ii) of Theorem 4.13, the group Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})) identifies with the centralizer of Inn⁡(Γ^​(S,∂S))/Inn⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S))≅Σn×Σk\operatorname{Inn}({\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\left/\operatorname{Inn}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\right.\cong\Sigma_{n}\times\Sigma_{k} in Out𝕀⁡(P​Γˇ​(S,∂S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})). This implies that the action of Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})) on ∏i=1kτδiℤ^\prod_{i=1}^{k}\tau_{{\delta}_{i}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} preserves the procyclic subgroup τδiℤ^\tau_{{\delta}_{i}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}, for i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k. Moreover, since these subgroups are all conjugated by the action of Inn⁡(Γ^​(S,∂S))\operatorname{Inn}({\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})), one of this action, say the one on τδ1ℤ^\tau_{{\delta}_{1}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}, determines them all. From (i) of Lemma 4.8, it then follows that there is a natural monomorphism:

(17) Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))↪Aut⁡(τδ1ℤ^)×Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S)).\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(\tau_{{\delta}_{1}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}})\times\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S)).

By the remarks above, the outer action of Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})) on P​Γˇ​(S,∂S){\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}) (cf. item (ii) of Theorem 4.13) preserves the kernel of the epimorphism P​Γˇ​(S,∂S)→P​Γˇ​(S′,∂S′){\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})\to{\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S^{\prime},{\partial S}^{\prime}), where we let S′:=S0,n+k−11S^{\prime}:=S_{0,n+k-1}^{1}. Therefore, the latter epimorphism induces a homomorphism Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(P​Γˇ​(S′,∂S′))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\check{\Gamma}}(S^{\prime},{\partial S}^{\prime})) and then, by (ii) of Theorem 4.13, a homomorphism:

(18) Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S′,∂S′)).\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S^{\prime},{\partial S}^{\prime})).

Let us observe that the component Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Aut⁡(τδ1ℤ^)\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Aut}(\tau_{{\delta}_{1}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}) of the monomorphism (17) factors through the homomorphism (18). By Lemma 6.4, this is then determined by the character χλ:GT^→ℤ^∗\chi_{\lambda}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\to{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast}. Hence, since, by the proof of item (i) of Theorem 6.1 in Section 6.2, we already know that Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}, it follows that the component Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))→Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S)) of the monomorphism (17) is injective. ∎

For S=Sg,nkS=S_{g,n}^{k} and d⁡(S)>1d(S)>1, by Lemma 6.5, Lemma 6.6 and the results of Section 6.2, there is a natural monomorphism:

R∅∘R0:Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))↪Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S0,n+2​gk))≅GT^.R_{\emptyset}\circ R_{0}\colon\thinspace\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S_{0,n+2g}^{k}))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}.

Thus, by Lemma 6.3, we get a series of natural monomorphisms:

GT^↪Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))↪GT^,\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\hookrightarrow\widehat{\operatorname{GT}},

from which we conclude that Out𝕀⁡(Γˇ​(S,∂S))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\check{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}. Item (iv) of Theorem 6.1 follows from the proof above as well.

6.4. The proof of Lemma 6.3

In the following sections, we will first prove a version of Lemma 6.3 for profinite mapping class groups in genus ≤2\leq 2. By the congruence subgroup property in genus ≤2\leq 2, this will complete the proof of Lemma 6.3 and thus of Theorem 6.1 for the genus ≤2\leq 2 case.

For higher genus, we will need first to answer an old open question in Grothendieck-Teichmüller theory, namely whether there exists a natural GT^\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}-action on the profinite mapping class group associated to every hyperbolic surface.

Let Aut𝕀0⁡(P​Γ^​(S))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S)) be the closed subgroup of Aut⁡(P​Γ^​(S))\operatorname{Aut}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S)) consisting of those elements which preserve the conjugacy class of a procyclic subgroup (topologically) generated by a Dehn twists about a nonseparating simple closed curve and by Out𝕀0⁡(P​Γ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S)) its quotient by the subgroup of inner automorphisms. We will prove that:

Theorem 6.7.

For SS a hyperbolic surface such that d⁡(S)>1d(S)>1, there is a natural faithful representation:

ρ^GT^:GT^↪Out𝕀0⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)).\hat{\rho}_{\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})).

This outer representation restricts to an action by automorphisms on the central inertia group ∏i=1kτδiℤ^\prod_{i=1}^{k}\tau_{{\delta}_{i}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} of P​Γ^​(S,∂S){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}) with the property that each procyclic subgroup τδiℤ^\tau_{{\delta}_{i}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} is preserved and acted upon through the character χλ:GT^→ℤ^∗\chi_{\lambda}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\to{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast}, for i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k.

The proof of Lemma 6.3 will then be obtained as a corollary of Theorem 6.7 (or better a corollary of its proof).

6.5. Profinite hyperelliptic mapping class groups

A hyperelliptic hyperbolic surface (S,υ)(S,{\upsilon}) is the datum of a hyperbolic surface SS and a hyperelliptic involution υ{\upsilon} on SS, that is to say, an involution such that the quotient surface Sυ:=S/⟨υ⟩S_{\upsilon}:=S/\langle{\upsilon}\rangle has genus 00. The hyperelliptic mapping class group Υ⁡(S){\Upsilon}(S) is then defined to be the centralizer of υ{\upsilon} in the mapping class group Γ⁡(S){\Gamma}(S). For 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} a finite subset of SS and 𝒫→\vec{\mathcal{P}} the same subset with a fixed order of its elements, we then let Γ⁡(S,𝒫)≅Γ⁡(S∖𝒫){\Gamma}(S,{\mathcal{P}})\cong{\Gamma}(S\smallsetminus{\mathcal{P}}) be the mapping class group of the marked surface (S,𝒫)(S,{\mathcal{P}}) and Γ⁡(S,𝒫→){\Gamma}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}) be the kernel of the natural representation Γ⁡(S,𝒫)→Σ𝒫{\Gamma}(S,{\mathcal{P}})\to\Sigma_{\mathcal{P}}.

The hyperelliptic mapping class groups Υ⁡(S,𝒫){\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) and Υ⁡(S,𝒫→){\Upsilon}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}) are, respectively, the inverse images of Υ⁡(S){\Upsilon}(S) by the epimorphisms Γ⁡(S,𝒫)→Γ⁡(S){\Gamma}(S,{\mathcal{P}})\to{\Gamma}(S) and Γ⁡(S,𝒫→)→Γ⁡(S){\Gamma}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})\to{\Gamma}(S).

The profinite hyperelliptic mapping class groups Υ^​(S,𝒫){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) and Υ^​(S,𝒫→){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}) are then, respectively, the profinite completions of Υ⁡(S,𝒫){\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) and Υ⁡(S,𝒫→){\Upsilon}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}). The congruence topology on Γ⁡(S,𝒫)≅Γ⁡(S∖𝒫){\Gamma}(S,{\mathcal{P}})\cong{\Gamma}(S\smallsetminus{\mathcal{P}}) induces a profinite topology on Υ⁡(S,𝒫){\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) and Υ⁡(S,𝒫→){\Upsilon}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}) via the embeddings Υ⁡(S,𝒫→)⊆Υ⁡(S,𝒫)⊆Γ⁡(S,𝒫){\Upsilon}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})\subseteq{\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}})\subseteq{\Gamma}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) also called the congruence topology. By [6, Theorem 7.2], this topology coincides with the full profinite topology. Hence, in the sequel, we will identify profinite and procongruence hyperelliptic mapping class groups.

6.6. The complex of symmetric profinite curves

A symmetric multicurve on a marked hyperelliptic surface (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) is a multicurve on S∖𝒫S\smallsetminus{\mathcal{P}} whose isotopy class in SS is preserved by the hyperelliptic involution υ{\upsilon}. The complex of symmetric curves C⁡(S,υ,𝒫)C(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) is the (abstract) simplicial complex whose simplices are the symmetric multicurves on (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) (cf. [6, Definition 2.7]). This is clearly a full subcomplex of the curve complex C⁡(S∖𝒫)C(S\smallsetminus{\mathcal{P}}). We then define the complex of symmetric profinite curves C^​(S,υ,𝒫){\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) on (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) to be the (abstract) simplicial profinite complex whose (profinite) set of kk-simplices is the closure of C​(S,υ,𝒫)kC(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}})_{k} inside Cˇ​(S∖𝒫)k{\check{C}}(S\smallsetminus{\mathcal{P}})_{k} (cf. [6, Definition 7.11], where this complex is denoted by L​(Π^​(S∖𝒫),υ)L({\widehat{\Pi}}(S\smallsetminus{\mathcal{P}}),{\upsilon})).

Simplices of C⁡(S,υ,𝒫)C(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) parameterize the multitwists of the hyperelliptic mapping class group Υ⁡(S,𝒫){\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) as well as the abelian subgroups generated by Dehn twists. In [6, Section 7.7], we showed that the simplices of C^​(S,υ,𝒫){\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) parameterize profinite multitwists in the profinite hyperelliptic mapping class group Υ^​(S,𝒫){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}}). In particular, for UU an open subgroup of Υ^​(S,𝒫){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) (which is then a closed subgroup of Γˇ​(S∖𝒫){\check{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\mathcal{P}})), the nontrivial decomposition and inertia groups UσU_{\sigma} and I^σ​(U){\hat{I}}_{\sigma}(U) of UU (cf. Definition 3.1 and Definition 3.3) are parameterized by C^​(S,υ,𝒫){\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}). The same arguments of the proofs of Proposition 7.2 and [7, Theorem 7.3, (ii)] show that there is a natural continuous homomorphism Aut𝔻⁡(U)→Aut⁡(C^​(S,υ,𝒫))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{D}}(U)\to\operatorname{Aut}({\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}})) whose kernel identifies with the abelian group Hom⁡(U/Z⁡(U),Z⁡(U))\operatorname{Hom}(U/Z(U),Z(U)). The usual argument then shows that this has trivial intersection with the subgroup Aut𝕀⁡(U)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}(U) of Aut𝔻⁡(U)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{D}}(U), so that there is a monomorphism Aut𝕀⁡(U)↪Aut⁡(C^​(S,υ,𝒫))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}(U)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}({\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}})).

It is likely that a version of [7, Theorem 5.5] holds in the hyperelliptic case. This would show, in particular, that the 𝕀\mathbb{I}-automorphisms of UU preserve the topological types of the inertia groups I^σ​(U){\hat{I}}_{\sigma}(U), for σ∈C^​(S,υ,𝒫){\sigma}\in{\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}). Since we will not need this result in the sequel, we instead give the following definition:

Definition 6.8.

For HH a closed subgroup of Υ^​(S,B){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,B), we let Aut𝕀top⁡(H)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}(H) be the closed subgroup of Aut𝕀⁡(H)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}(H) consisting of those elements which preserve the topological types of the inertia groups of HH. We then say that a subgroup KK of HH is 𝕀top\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}-characteristic if it is preserved by Aut𝕀top⁡(H)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}(H). Note that Inn⁡(U)≤Aut𝕀top⁡(U)\operatorname{Inn}(U)\leq\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}(U), for UU an open subgroup of Υ^​(S,𝒫){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}}), so that, in particular, an 𝕀top\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}-characteristic subgroup of UU is normal.

For the closed surface case, we have the following result:

Proposition 6.9.

For SS a closed surface of genus g≥2g\geq 2, endowed with a hyperelliptic involution υ{\upsilon}, there is a natural isomorphism Out⁡(Υ^​(S))≅{±1}×Out𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))\cong\{\pm 1\}\times\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) and a series of natural isomorphisms:

(19) Out𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))=Out𝕀0⁡(Υ^​(S))≅Out⁡(Γ^0,[2​g+2])≅GT^.\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))=\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))\cong\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Gamma}}_{0,[2g+2]})\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}.

In particular, we have Aut𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))=Aut𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))=\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)).

Proof.

By [7, Lemma 7.4], there is an exact sequence:

1→Hom⁡(Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S)),Z⁡(Υ^​(S)))→Out⁡(Υ^​(S))→Out⁡(Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S))),1\to\operatorname{Hom}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)),Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)))\to\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))\to\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))),

where Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S))≅Γ^0,[2​g+2]{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))\cong{\widehat{\Gamma}}_{0,[2g+2]} and the center Z​(Υ^​(S))Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) is generated by the hyperelliptic involution υ{\upsilon}. Since the abelianization of Γ^0,[2​g+2]{\widehat{\Gamma}}_{0,[2g+2]} is isomorphic to ℤ/2​(2​g+1)\mathbb{Z}/2(2g+1) (cf. [10, § 5.1.3]), we have that Hom⁡(Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S)),Z⁡(Υ^​(S)))≅{±1}\operatorname{Hom}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)),Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)))\cong\{\pm 1\}.

By the usual argument, the image of Hom⁡(Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S)),Z⁡(Υ^​(S)))\operatorname{Hom}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)),Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))) in Out⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) has trivial intersection with the subgroups Out𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) and Out𝕀0⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) of the latter group.

Since Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S))=Γ^0,[2​g+2]{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))={\widehat{\Gamma}}_{0,[2g+2]}, from Lemma 3.13 and [8, Lemma 6.7], it then follows that the image of Out⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) in Out⁡(Υ^​(S)/Z​(Υ^​(S)))\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))) identifies with the images there of both its subgroups Out𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) and Out𝕀0⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)). This implies that there is an isomorphism Out⁡(Υ^​(S))≅{±1}×Out𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))\cong\{\pm 1\}\times\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) and also the identity Out𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))=Out𝕀0⁡(Υ^​(S))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))=\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)).

Let (S∘,υ)(S^{\circ},{\upsilon}) be the hyperelliptic surface with boundary obtained from the hyperelliptic surface (S,υ)(S,{\upsilon}) by replacing one of the Weierstrass points with a circle. The Birman-Hilden theorem states that there is a natural isomorphism ZΓ⁡(S∘,∂S∘)​(υ)≅B2​g+1Z_{{\Gamma}(S^{\circ},\partial S^{\circ})}({\upsilon})\cong B_{2g+1}, where B2​g+1B_{2g+1} is Artin braid group. Moreover, if zz is the standard generator of the (cyclic) center of B2​g+1B_{2g+1}, this isomorphism induces an isomorphism Υ⁡(S)≅B2​g+1/⟨z2⟩{\Upsilon}(S)\cong B_{2g+1}/\langle z^{2}\rangle (cf. [10, Chapter 9]).

In [19, Appendix 4], Ihara showed that there is an action of the profinite Grothendieck-Teichmüller group GT^\widehat{\operatorname{GT}} on the profinite completion B^n\widehat{B}_{n} of the Artin braid group BnB_{n}, for all n≥3n\geq 3, which preserves the conjugacy class of the procyclic subgroups generated by the standard braids. The Birman-Hilden theorem then implies that there is a representation GT^→Out𝕀0⁡(Υ^​(S))\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)) compatible with the natural monomorphism Out𝕀0⁡(Υ^​(S))↪Out⁡(Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S)))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{0}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))) and the isomorphism Out⁡(Υ^​(S)/Z⁡(Υ^​(S)))≅GT^\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)/Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S)))\cong\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}. This yields the series of isomorphisms (19). The last claim then follows from the isomorphism Out𝕀⁡(Υ^​(S))≅Out⁡(Γ^0,[2​g+2])\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S))\cong\operatorname{Out}({\widehat{\Gamma}}_{0,[2g+2]}) and Lemma 3.13. ∎

6.7. Modular subgroups of the hyperelliptic mapping class group

The definition of hyperelliptic mapping class groups makes sense also when (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) is a marked disconnected hyperelliptic surface (cf. [6, Section 2.8 and 2.9]). For instance, for γ{\gamma} a symmetric simple closed curve on (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}), the marked hyperelliptic surface (S∖γ,υ,𝒫)(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) is a possibly disconnected marked hyperelliptic surface. Let us label by Q+,Q−Q_{+},Q_{-} the pair of punctures on S∖γS\smallsetminus{\gamma} bounded by γ{\gamma} and denote by Υ​(S∖γ,𝒫){Q+,Q−}{\Upsilon}(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\mathcal{P}})_{\{Q_{+},Q_{-}\}} the stabilizer of this pair of punctures for the action of Υ⁡(S∖γ,𝒫){\Upsilon}(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\mathcal{P}}) on the set of all punctures of S∖γS\smallsetminus{\gamma}. The stabilizer Υ​(S,𝒫)γ{\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma} for the action of the hyperelliptic mapping class group Υ⁡(S,𝒫){\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) on the set C​(S,υ,𝒫)0C(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}})_{0} is then described by the short exact sequence (cf. the short exact sequence (14) in [6]):

1→τγℤ→Υ​(S,𝒫)γ→Υ​(S∖γ,𝒫){Q+,Q−}→1.1\to\tau_{\gamma}^{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma}\to{\Upsilon}(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\mathcal{P}})_{\{Q_{+},Q_{-}\}}\to 1.

A similar short exact sequence also describes the stabilizer Υ​(S,𝒫→)γ{\Upsilon}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma}.

In [6, Section 7.6], the above description of stabilizers is extended to profinite hyperelliptic mapping class group. More precisely, for γ{\gamma} a symmetric simple closed curve on (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}), which we now regard as an element of the profinite set C^​(S,υ,𝒫)0{\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}})_{0}, the stabilizer Υ^​(S,𝒫)γ{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma} for the action of Υ^​(S,𝒫){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}}) on C​(S,υ,𝒫)0C(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}})_{0} is described by the short exact sequence (cf. [6, Corollary 7.8]):

1→τγℤ^→Υ^​(S,𝒫)γ→Υ^​(S∖γ,𝒫){Q+,Q−}→1,1\to\tau_{\gamma}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma}\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\mathcal{P}})_{\{Q_{+},Q_{-}\}}\to 1,

where Υ^​(S,𝒫)γ{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma} and Υ^​(S∖γ,𝒫){Q+,Q−}{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\mathcal{P}})_{\{Q_{+},Q_{-}\}} are naturally isomorphic to the profinite completions of the groups Υ​(S,𝒫)γ{\Upsilon}(S,{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma} and Υ​(S∖γ,𝒫){Q+,Q−}{\Upsilon}(S\smallsetminus{\gamma},{\mathcal{P}})_{\{Q_{+},Q_{-}\}}, respectively. Again, a similar description holds for the stabilizer Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma}.

For the applications in this paper, we are more interested in the case when γ{\gamma} is a nonseparating simple closed curve and the set of marked points 𝒫{\mathcal{P}} is ordered. Therefore, we will give a more precise description of the stabilizer in this case.

For SS a closed surface and γ{\gamma} a nonseparating symmetric simple closed curve on (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}), let Sγ:=S∖γS_{\gamma}:=S\smallsetminus{\gamma} and let Υ​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘{\Upsilon}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ} be the index 22 subgroup of Υ⁡(Sγ,𝒫→){\Upsilon}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}}) consisting of those elements which do not swap the punctures of SγS_{\gamma} labeled by Q+Q_{+} and Q−Q_{-} (this is also described as the kernel of the natural representation Υ⁡(Sγ,𝒫→)→Σ{Q+,Q−}{\Upsilon}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})\to\Sigma_{\{Q_{+},Q_{-}\}}). The stabilizer Υ​(S,𝒫→)γ→{\Upsilon}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}} of the oriented simple closed curve γ→\vec{\gamma} is described by the short exact sequence:

1→τγℤ→Υ​(S,𝒫→)γ→→Υ​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘→1.1\to\tau_{\gamma}^{\mathbb{Z}}\to{\Upsilon}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}}\to{\Upsilon}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ}\to 1.

Let NγN_{\gamma} be the normal subgroup of Υ​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘{\Upsilon}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ} generated by the Dehn twists about symmetric separating simple closed curves on (Sγ,υ,𝒫)(S_{\gamma},{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) bounding a disc which contains no marked points and only the two punctures labeled by Q+Q_{+} and Q−Q_{-} and let S¯γ\overline{S}_{\gamma} be the surface obtained from SγS_{\gamma} by filling in the the punctures on SγS_{\gamma} labeled by Q+Q_{+} and Q−Q_{-} with two points (which we also label by Q+Q_{+} and Q−Q_{-}). The group Υ​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘{\Upsilon}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ} then fits in the short exact sequence (cf. [6, Theorem 3.1]):

1→Nγ→Υ​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘→Υ⁡(S¯γ,𝒫∪Q+→)→1.1\to N_{\gamma}\to{\Upsilon}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ}\to{\Upsilon}(\overline{S}_{\gamma},\overrightarrow{{\mathcal{P}}\cup Q_{+}})\to 1.

From the above results, it follows:

Proposition 6.10.

Let (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) be a marked hyperelliptic hyperbolic surface and γ{\gamma} a symmetric nonseparating simple closed curve on (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}). With the above notations, we have:

  1. (i)

    The stabilizer Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma} for the action of Υ^​(S,𝒫→){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}) on the profinite set C^​(S,υ,𝒫)0{\widehat{C}}(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}})_{0} is described by the two short exact sequences:

    1→Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ→→Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ→ϵ{±1}→1and 1→τγℤ^→Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ→→Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘→1,\begin{array}[]{ll}&1\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}}\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\epsilon}}{{\to}}\{\pm 1\}\to 1\\ \mbox{and }&\\ &1\to\tau_{\gamma}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}}\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ}\to 1,\end{array}

    where ϵ\epsilon is the orientation character associated to the curve γ{\gamma} and Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ} is the kernel of the natural representation Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)→Σ{Q+,Q−}{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})\to\Sigma_{\{Q_{+},Q_{-}\}}.

  2. (ii)

    The profinite group Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ} fits in the short exact sequence:

    1→N¯γ→Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘→Υ^​(S¯γ,𝒫∪Q+→)→1,1\to\overline{N}_{\gamma}\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ}\to{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(\overline{S}_{\gamma},\overrightarrow{{\mathcal{P}}\cup Q_{+}})\to 1,

    where N¯γ\overline{N}_{\gamma} is the closure of the group NγN_{\gamma} in the profinite group Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫){\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},{\mathcal{P}}).

6.8. Homomorphisms between outer automorphism groups of profinite hyperelliptic mapping class groups

Let (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) be a marked hyperelliptic closed surface of genus g≥2g\geq 2 and γ{\gamma} a symmetric nonseparating simple closed curve on (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}). The subgroup Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ→{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}} of Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\gamma} is 𝕀top\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}-characteristic. By the same construction of the homomorphism (6), there is then a natural homomorphism:

Aut𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→))→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ→).\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}}).

From [6, Theorem 7.13], for g≥2g\geq 2, it follows that Z⁡(Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘)={1}Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ})=\{1\}. Hence, by (i) of Proposition 6.10, we have OPENZ⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ→))=τγℤ^Z({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}}))=\tau_{\gamma}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} and there is a natural homomorphism:

Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→)γ→)→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘)\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\vec{\gamma}})\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ})

By composing the two above homomorphisms, we then get the homomorphism:

(20) Aut𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→))→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘).\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ}).

The subgroup N¯γ\overline{N}_{\gamma} of Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ} (cf. (ii) of Proposition 6.10) is (topologically) generated by the profinite Dehn twists about symmetric profinite curves on (Sγ,υ,𝒫)(S_{\gamma},{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) of topological type a simple closed curve bounding a disc which only contains the two punctures labeled by Q+Q_{+} and Q−Q_{-}. Therefore, N¯γ\overline{N}_{\gamma} is an 𝕀top{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}-characteristic subgroup of Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘{\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ} and there is a natural homomorphism Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(Sγ,𝒫→)∘)→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S¯γ,𝒫∪Q+→))\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S_{\gamma},\vec{\mathcal{P}})_{\circ})\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(\overline{S}_{\gamma},\overrightarrow{{\mathcal{P}}\cup Q_{+}})). Composing the latter with the homomorphism (20), we get a natural homomorphism:

Aut𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→))→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S¯γ,𝒫∪Q+→)).\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(\overline{S}_{\gamma},\overrightarrow{{\mathcal{P}}\cup Q_{+}})).

It is not difficult to see that the kernel of this homomorphism contains Inn⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→))\operatorname{Inn}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})). Therefore, there is a natural homomorphism:

(21) Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→))→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S¯γ,𝒫∪Q+→)).\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(\overline{S}_{\gamma},\overrightarrow{{\mathcal{P}}\cup Q_{+}})).
Proposition 6.11.

For (S,υ,𝒫)(S,{\upsilon},{\mathcal{P}}) a marked hyperelliptic closed surface of genus g≥2g\geq 2, there is a natural representation:

Φ(S,𝒫→):GT^→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→)).\Phi_{(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})).
Proof.

Let n:=♯​𝒫n:=\sharp{\mathcal{P}} and let σ:={γ1,…,γn}{\sigma}:=\{{\gamma}_{1},\ldots,{\gamma}_{n}\} be a set of disjoint symmetric closed curves on a hyperelliptic closed surface (S′,υ)(S^{\prime},{\upsilon}) of genus g+ng+n such that Sσ′:=S′∖σS^{\prime}_{\sigma}:=S^{\prime}\smallsetminus{\sigma} is connected. Then, (Sσ′,υ)(S^{\prime}_{\sigma},{\upsilon}) is a hyperelliptic surface endowed with nn pairs of symmetric punctures (with respect to the hyperelliptic involution υ{\upsilon}). Let (S,υ)(S,{\upsilon}) be the hyperelliptic closed surface obtained filling the 2​n2n punctures on Sσ′S^{\prime}_{\sigma} with the set of points 𝒫∪υ⁡(𝒫){\mathcal{P}}\cup{\upsilon}({\mathcal{P}}). Then, composing the nn homomorphism of type (21) associated, recursively, to the set of disjoint symmetric closed curves σ{\sigma} (note that each step adds a marked point out of the set 𝒫{\mathcal{P}}), by Proposition 6.9, we get the representation:

Φ(S,𝒫→):GT^≅Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S′))→Out𝕀top⁡(Υ^​(S,𝒫→)).\Phi_{(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\cong\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S^{\prime}))\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{top}}}({\widehat{\Upsilon}}(S,\vec{\mathcal{P}})).

∎

Corollary 6.12.

For S=S2,nS=S_{2,n} and all n≥0n\geq 0, there is a natural representation:

ΨS:GT^→Out𝕀⁡(Γ^​(S)).\Psi_{S}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\to\operatorname{Out}^{\mathbb{I}}({\widehat{\Gamma}}(S)).
Proof.

6.12. A presentation for the profinite relative mapping class group of a surface

In [11], Gervais gave a finite presentation of the pure mapping class group of a surface with boundary. In this section, we will show that this result implies that the profinite pure mapping class group of an open surface admits a presentation as a quotient of a profinite amalgamated product of stabilizers of oriented nonseparating simple closed curves by a few simple commutator relations.

For a finite set of groups G1,…,GkG_{1},\ldots,G_{k} and monomorphisms H↪GiH\hookrightarrow G_{i}, for i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k, we denote by ⊛Hi=1,…​kGi\bigoasterisk_{H}^{i=1,\ldots k}G_{i} their amalgamated free product with amalgamated subgroup HH. If the groups G1,…,Gk,HG_{1},\ldots,G_{k},H are profinite and the monomorphisms H↪GiH\hookrightarrow G_{i} continuous, we denote by ∐Hi=1,…​kGi\coprod_{H}^{i=1,\ldots k}G_{i} their amalgamated free profinite product with amalgamated subgroup HH (cf. [26, Section 9.2]). With the above notations, we have:

Proposition 6.13.

Let S=SgkS=S_{g}^{k} with k≥1k\geq 1 and g≥3g\geq 3, let σ={γ1,…,γg−1}{\sigma}=\{{\gamma}_{1},\ldots,{\gamma}_{g-1}\} be a set of disjoint simple closed curves on SS such that S∖σS\smallsetminus{\sigma} is connected and σ′={β1,…,βg−1}{\sigma}^{\prime}=\{\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{g-1}\} a set of disjoint simple closed curves such that S∖σ′S\smallsetminus{\sigma}^{\prime} is connected and the intersection βi∩γj\beta_{i}\cap{\gamma}_{j} is a single point for i=ji=j and empty otherwise. Let σi:=σ∖{γi}{\sigma}_{i}:={\sigma}\smallsetminus\{{\gamma}_{i}\}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1.

There is then a natural epimorphism:

Θ:⊛P​Γ​(S,∂S)σ→i=1,…,g−1PΓ(S,∂S)σ→i↠PΓ(S,∂S),\Theta\colon\thinspace\bigoasterisk_{{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{\sigma}}}^{i=1,\ldots,g-1}{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}\twoheadrightarrow{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S}),

whose kernel is normally generated by the commutators [τβi,τβj][\tau_{\beta_{i}},\tau_{\beta_{j}}], for i,j=1,…,g−1i,j=1,\ldots,g-1.

Proof.

The proposition is a consequence of [11, Theorem 1]. Let the curves {β1,…,βg−1}\{\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{g-1}\} in the statement of the proposition correspond to the curves denoted with the same letters in [11, Fig. 1]. Let instead γi{\gamma}_{i} be a simple closed curve contained in the handle of the surface in [11, Fig. 1] through which βi\beta_{i} passes and such that γi{\gamma}_{i} intersects βi\beta_{i} in a single point, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1. In particular, γi{\gamma}_{i} does not intersect any other curve in the set 𝒢g,n{\mathscr{G}}_{g,n} defined in [11], for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1.

Let us denote by GΘG_{\Theta} the quotient of the group ⊛P​Γ​(S,∂S)σ→i=1,…,g−1PΓ(S,∂S)σ→i\bigoasterisk_{{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{\sigma}}}^{i=1,\ldots,g-1}{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}} by the subgroup normally generated by the commutators [τβi,τβj][\tau_{\beta_{i}},\tau_{\beta_{j}}], for i,j=1,…,g−1i,j=1,\ldots,g-1. Since the group P​Γ​(S,∂S){\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S}) is generated by the union of the subgroups P​Γ​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1, we have that Θ\Theta is surjective and descends to an epimorphism Θ¯:GΘ→P​Γ​(S,∂S)\overline{\Theta}\colon\thinspace G_{\Theta}\to{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S}), such that its restriction to the subgroup P​Γ​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}} is injective for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1.

With the notations of [11, Theorem 1] (except that our ”kk” corresponds to the ”nn” in Gervais’ notation), let FF be the free group in the letters b,b1,…,bg−1b,b_{1},\dots,b_{g-1}, a1,…,a2​g+k−2a_{1},\dots,a_{2g+k-2}, {ci,j}\{c_{i,j}\}. Sending these elements to the images of the corresponding Dehn twists in GΘG_{\Theta} then defines a homomorphism H:F→GΘ\Eta\colon\thinspace F\to G_{\Theta}. Since, with the exception of the ”disjointness relations” τβi​τβj=τβj​τβi\tau_{\beta_{i}}\tau_{\beta_{j}}=\tau_{\beta_{j}}\tau_{\beta_{i}}, all relations in the presentation given in [11, Theorem 1] are supported on some subsurface S∖σiS\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1, of SS, the homomorphism H\Eta induces a homomorphism H¯:P​Γ​(S,∂S)→GΘ\overline{\Eta}\colon\thinspace{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})\to G_{\Theta}, such that its restriction to the subgroup P​Γ​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}} is injective for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1. In particular, H¯\overline{\Eta} is surjective and so the composition Θ¯∘H¯\overline{\Theta}\circ\overline{\Eta} is also surjective. Since the mapping class group P​Γ​(S,∂S){\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S,{\partial S}) is finitely generated and residually finite, it is Hopfian, so that Θ¯∘H¯\overline{\Theta}\circ\overline{\Eta} is an isomorphism. This implies that Θ¯\overline{\Theta} is an isomorphism as well. ∎

Remark 6.14.

After a careful reading of the paper [11], I noted a gap in the proof of [11, Lemma 8] where the author claims: ”Pasting a pair of pants to γ2​g+n−3,1{\gamma}_{2g+n-3,1} allows us to view Σg,n−1\Sigma_{g,n-1} as a subsurface of Σg,n\Sigma_{g,n}”. But this makes sense only for n>1n>1, which means that the proof of [11, Theorem 1] is complete only for n≥1n\geq 1. This is the reason why, in Proposition 6.13, we assume k≥1k\geq 1.

By the congruence subgroup property in genus ≤2\leq 2 and (ii) of Theorem 2.3, the closures of the subgroups P​Γ​(S)σ→{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S)_{\vec{\sigma}} and P​Γ​(S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\Gamma}(S)_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1, in the profinite mapping class group P​Γ^​(S){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S) identify with their respective profinite completions. Therefore, by the universal property of amalgamated free profinite products (cf. [26, Section 9.2]), we have:

Corollary 6.15.

With the notations of Proposition 6.13, there is a natural continuous epimorphism:

Θ^:∐P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i=1,…,g−1P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i↠P​Γ^​(S,∂S),\widehat{\Theta}\colon\thinspace\coprod_{{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{\sigma}}}^{i=1,\ldots,g-1}{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}\twoheadrightarrow{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}),

whose kernel is (topologically) normally generated by the commutators [τβi,τβj][\tau_{\beta_{i}},\tau_{\beta_{j}}], for i,j=1,…,g−1i,j=1,\ldots,g-1.

Therefore, the quotient of P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}} by its center CC is isomorphic to P​Γ^​(S∖σi){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i}) and there is a natural homomorphism, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1:

(26) Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)→Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S∖σi)).\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}})\to\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})).
Lemma 6.17.

The homomorphism (26) is injective.

Proof.

Let us consider the wreath products ℤ^∗≀Σk{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast}\wr\Sigma_{k} and ℤ^∗≀Σg−2{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast}\wr\Sigma_{g-2} and their respective canonical primitive actions on ∏j=1kτδjℤ^\prod_{j=1}^{k}\tau_{\delta_{j}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} and ∏l=1,…​i^​…,g−1τγlℤ^\prod_{l=1,\dots\hat{i}\dots,g-1}\tau_{{\gamma}_{l}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}.

The natural action of Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}) on CC factors through the above canonical actions and a natural homomorphism:

Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)→(ℤ^∗≀Σk)×(ℤ^∗≀Σg−2).\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}})\to({\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast}\wr\Sigma_{k})\times({\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast}\wr\Sigma_{g-2}).

Let us then observe that this homomorphism can be recovered from:

  • •

    a natural character Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)→Aut⁡(τδ1ℤ^)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}})\to\operatorname{Aut}(\tau_{\delta_{1}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}), which, by the above construction and the case g≤2g\leq 2 of Theorem 6.1, is determined by the character χλ:GT^→ℤ^∗\chi_{\lambda}\colon\thinspace\widehat{\operatorname{GT}}\to{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}^{\ast};

  • •

    a natural character Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)→Aut⁡(τγ1ℤ^)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}})\to\operatorname{Aut}(\tau_{{\gamma}_{1}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}), which is determined by the homomorphism (26) and a natural character Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S∖σi))→Aut⁡(τγℤ^)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i}))\to\operatorname{Aut}(\tau_{{\gamma}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}), where γ{\gamma} is a nonseparating simple closed curve on S∖σiS\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i};

  • •

    a natural epimorphism Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)→Σk×Σg−2\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}})\to\Sigma_{k}\times\Sigma_{g-2} which can be recovered from the homomorphism (26) and the epimorphism Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S∖σi))→Σk+2​g−4\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i}))\to\Sigma_{k+2g-4} (cf. (ii) of Theorem 4.1).

The above remarks imply that the action of Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}) on CC is determined by the homomorphism (26). Since, by [7, Lemma 7.4] and the same argument of the proof of Lemma 4.8, the natural homomorphism:

Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i)→Aut⁡(C)×Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S∖σi))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}})\to\operatorname{Aut}(C)\times\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i}))

is injective, it follows that the homomorphism (26) is already injective. ∎

Let us now denote, respectively, by f̊i\ring{f}_{i} and f̊i′\ring{f}_{i}^{\prime} the images in Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S∖σi))\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})) of the elements f~i\tilde{f}_{i} and f~i′\tilde{f}_{i}^{\prime} defined above by the monomorphism (26).

By hypothesis, f~i′⋅f~i−1\tilde{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\tilde{f}_{i}^{-1} restricts to the identity on the subgroup P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{\sigma}} and so induces the identity automorphism on the quotient P​Γ^​(S∖σi)γ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})_{\vec{\gamma}_{i}} of this subgroup. From (i) of Lemma 5.6, it then follows that f̊i′⋅f̊i−1∈Inn⁡(Γ^​(S∖σi))\ring{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\ring{f}_{i}^{-1}\in\operatorname{Inn}({\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})).

By construction, f̊i′⋅f̊i−1\ring{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\ring{f}_{i}^{-1} preserves the inertia group I^γi{\hat{I}}_{{\gamma}_{i}}. Hence, f̊i′⋅f̊i−1∈Inn⁡(Γ^​(S∖σi)γi)\ring{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\ring{f}_{i}^{-1}\in\operatorname{Inn}({\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})_{{\gamma}_{i}}), where the latter group is identified with a subgroup of Inn⁡(Γ^​(S∖σi))⊂Aut𝕀⁡(P​Γ^​(S∖σi))\operatorname{Inn}({\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i}))\subset\operatorname{Aut}^{\mathbb{I}}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})).

Above, we observed that f~i′⋅f~i−1\tilde{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\tilde{f}_{i}^{-1} induces the identity on P​Γ^​(S∖σi)γ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})_{\vec{\gamma}_{i}} and so f̊i′⋅f̊i−1\ring{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\ring{f}_{i}^{-1} identifies with an inner automorphism of Γ^​(S∖σi)γi{\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})_{{\gamma}_{i}} which restricts to the identity on P​Γ^​(S∖σi)γ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S\smallsetminus{\sigma}_{i})_{\vec{\gamma}_{i}}. By [7, Theorem 4.14], this implies that f̊i′⋅f̊i−1=1\ring{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\ring{f}_{i}^{-1}=1. Since the homomorphism (26) is injective, it follows that f~i′⋅f~i−1=1\tilde{f}_{i}^{\prime}\cdot\tilde{f}_{i}^{-1}=1 and then f~i′=f~i\tilde{f}_{i}^{\prime}=\tilde{f}_{i}. ∎

The automorphisms f~i\tilde{f}_{i}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1, then glue to an automorphism:

F~∈Aut⁡(∐P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i=1,…,g−1P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i).\tilde{F}\in\operatorname{Aut}(\coprod_{{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{\sigma}}}^{i=1,\ldots,g-1}{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}).
Lemma 6.18.

With the notations of Corollary 6.15, there holds F~​(ker⁡Θ^)⊆ker⁡Θ^\tilde{F}(\ker\widehat{\Theta})\subseteq\ker\widehat{\Theta}.

Proof.

By Corollary 6.15, it is enough to prove that there holds F~​([τβi,τβj])∈ker⁡Θ^\tilde{F}([\tau_{\beta_{i}},\tau_{\beta_{j}}])\in\ker\widehat{\Theta}, for i,j=1,…,g−1i,j=1,\ldots,g-1. Letting F¯:=Θ^∘F~\underline{F}:=\widehat{\Theta}\circ\tilde{F}, this is equivalent to the identity F¯​([τβi,τβj])=[F¯​(τβi),F¯​(τβj)]=1\underline{F}([\tau_{\beta_{i}},\tau_{\beta_{j}}])=[\underline{F}(\tau_{\beta_{i}}),\underline{F}(\tau_{\beta_{j}})]=1, for i,j=1,…,g−1i,j=1,\ldots,g-1, and so to the fact that the element F¯​(τβi)\underline{F}(\tau_{\beta_{i}}) commutes with F¯​(τβj)\underline{F}(\tau_{\beta_{j}}) in the profinite mapping class group P​Γ^​(S,∂S){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}), for i,j=1,…,g−1i,j=1,\ldots,g-1.

Let us recall that SαiS_{\alpha_{i}} is the compact genus 11 subsurface of SS with boundary αi\alpha_{i} which contains the simple closed curve βi\beta_{i}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1.

By (i) of Theorem 2.3 and the subgoup congruence property for mapping class groups in genus ≤2\leq 2, there are natural monomorphisms P​Γ^​(Sαi,αi)↪P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S_{\alpha_{i}},\alpha_{i})\hookrightarrow{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}. Let us identify P​Γ^​(Sαi,αi){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S_{\alpha_{i}},\alpha_{i}) with its image in P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1.

We defined the automorphism f~i\tilde{f}_{i} of P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}} in such a way that it preserves the procyclic subgroup ταiℤ^\tau_{\alpha_{i}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}}. Thus, f~i\tilde{f}_{i} also preserves the normalizer of ταiℤ^\tau_{\alpha_{i}}^{\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}} in P​Γ^​(S,∂S)σ→i{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})_{\vec{{\sigma}}_{i}}. By Theorem 2.8, f~i\tilde{f}_{i} then preserves the subgroup P​Γ^​(Sαi,αi){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S_{\alpha_{i}},\alpha_{i}) (which contains the element τβi\tau_{\beta_{i}}), for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1.

Since, inside P​Γ^​(S,∂S){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S}), for i≠ji\neq j, all elements of the subgroup P​Γ^​(Sαi,αi){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S_{\alpha_{i}},\alpha_{i}) commute with all elements of the subgroup P​Γ^​(Sαj,αj){\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S_{\alpha_{j}},\alpha_{j}), it follows that F¯​(τβi)∈P​Γ^​(Sαi,αi)\underline{F}(\tau_{\beta_{i}})\in{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S_{\alpha_{i}},\alpha_{i}) commutes with F¯​(τβj)∈P​Γ^​(Sαj,αj)\underline{F}(\tau_{\beta_{j}})\in{\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S_{\alpha_{j}},\alpha_{j}) for i,j=1,…,g−1i,j=1,\ldots,g-1, which concludes the proof of the lemma. ∎

By the Hopfian property of (topologically) finitely generated profinite groups, Corollary 6.15 and Lemma 6.18 imply that F~\tilde{F} descends to an automorphism F¯∈Aut⁡(P​Γ^​(S,∂S))\bar{F}\in\operatorname{Aut}({\mathrm{P}\widehat{\Gamma}}(S,{\partial S})). Moreover, by definition, F¯\bar{F} preserve the inertia groups I^γi{\hat{I}}_{{\gamma}_{i}}, for i=1,…,g−1i=1,\ldots,g-1.
